teachingBlocks.title: Orientation and Safety
teachingBlocks.objective: Use audible movement calls and basic line-safety habits before moving through a live station.
teachingBlocks.canonicalSolution:
Prompt: You are walking from the dish pit back to your station carrying a hot sauté pan in your right hand and a knife in your left. Three coworkers are on the line. List exactly what you say, in order, between leaving the dish pit and arriving at your station.

Expected response:
1. 'Hot, sharp, behind' as you start moving
2. 'Corner' at every blind corner you pass
3. 'Behind' as you pass each coworker

Success criteria:
1. Cook calls hot, sharp, and behind before moving — not during or after.
2. Cook calls corner at blind corners every time, not selectively.
3. Cook does not lower their voice; calls are made to be heard.
teachingBlocks.explanation:
Set the floor for every shift. Before any cook touches a knife or a pan on a live line, they have to understand that safety is the default state of the work, not an interruption to it.

The cook can recite the four most common line hazards, demonstrate the safe response to each, and explain why calling movement out loud is faster, not slower, than working in silence.

On a working line, the only way to move six bodies through a five-foot space without injuries is to make movement audible. Hot, sharp, behind, corner — these are not optional manners; they are the system that lets cooks turn quickly without looking. A cook who does not call is a cook who will be hit, or who will hit someone else. Falling knives are never caught. Hot pans are flagged the moment they leave the burner. A cook who internalizes this stops thinking about it during service, and that is the goal.

Source data note: Generic line-safety standards. Uncle Julio's specific safety reporting chain, on-site emergency procedures, and any brand-specific call vocabulary need authorized source for production use.

teachingBlocks.title: Tools and Color Barriers
teachingBlocks.objective: Use industry-standard color barriers and dedicated tools to prevent cross-contact during prep and service.
teachingBlocks.canonicalSolution:
Prompt: You are setting up to portion four items: raw chicken thighs, sliced tomato, cooked carnitas, and raw shrimp. Match each item to the correct cutting-board color using the industry-standard mapping. Then explain what you do if the yellow board is in the dish pit.

Expected response:
1. raw chicken thighs:yellow
2. sliced tomato:green
3. cooked carnitas:brown
4. raw shrimp:blue
5. fallback:wash-rinse-sanitize an alternate board, document the substitution, and replace the missing board to par before next service

Success criteria:
1. All four boards mapped correctly.
2. Fallback procedure includes wash-rinse-sanitize and a notation step, not just substitution.
3. Cook does not skip the documentation step; a missing board today is a missing board tomorrow.
teachingBlocks.explanation:
Get a cook fluent in the color-coded separation system that prevents cross-contamination. A cook who picks up the wrong colored board on a busy line is one ticket away from a recall conversation.

The cook can name the standard color-board mapping, identify the correct board for the protein in front of them, and explain what to do when the right color is not available.

Color-coded boards are the most low-tech and most effective cross-contamination control in any kitchen. The mapping is industry-standard for a reason: a cook switching from raw poultry to ready-to-eat product cannot rely on cleaning to be perfect mid-rush. Color separation makes the wrong move physically obvious. When a board is missing, the right answer is never 'use any board' — it is wash-rinse-sanitize a substitute, flag it on the prep board so it gets replaced, and tell the lead. Allergen (purple) tools are dedicated; they do not enter the general dish rotation during service because a single trace cross-contact event is the kind of mistake that ends careers.

Source data note: Industry-standard color mapping shown. Uncle Julio's may have additional internal mappings (tortilla press, salsa station, fajita prep) that need authorized source.

teachingBlocks.title: Station Setup
teachingBlocks.objective: Bring a cold station to ready in a repeatable order that protects sanitation, equipment readiness, and lead visibility.
teachingBlocks.canonicalSolution:
Prompt: Your station is cold. You have 12 minutes until first ticket. Put these eight steps in the correct order: stage tools, wipe and sanitize surfaces, mix sanitizer bucket, verify equipment temperature, confirm cutting board color matches assigned protein, stock rail to par in FIFO order, wash hands and check apron, tell the lead the station is up.

Expected response:
1. wash hands and check apron
2. wipe and sanitize surfaces
3. confirm cutting board color matches assigned protein
4. verify equipment temperature
5. mix sanitizer bucket
6. stock rail to par in FIFO order
7. stage tools
8. tell the lead the station is up

Success criteria:
1. Hand-wash is first, every time.
2. Surface sanitation comes before any food contact.
3. Equipment temperature verified by thermometer, not by sight.
4. Readiness call goes to the lead; the cook does not self-declare ready.
teachingBlocks.explanation:
Bring a cold station up to ready in the right order, the same way every time, so nothing is missed and nothing is rushed at the wrong time.

The cook can perform a station open without a checklist, can call readiness through the lead instead of self-declaring, and can identify what cannot be verified by sight alone.

A station open is layered: clean hands, clean surface, correct board, correct equipment temperature, correct sanitizer, correct stock, correct tool placement, and a public readiness call. Every layer is a defense. Cooks who freelance the order eventually skip a layer, and the kitchen finds out the hard way. The readiness call goes through the lead because cooks are biased reporters of their own readiness; the lead is the one who sees the whole line and confirms whether the station is actually ready to take a ticket. Calling readiness through the lead is not bureaucracy — it is how the line stays in sync.

Source data note: Generic open. Uncle Julio's specific open sheet, par sheet, station-specific equipment warmup (mesquite grill, tortilla press, salsa station), and brand-specific readiness markers need authorized source.

teachingBlocks.title: Line Readiness
teachingBlocks.objective: Turn an open station into a service-ready station by reading load signals, positioning stock, and escalating short-item risk early.
teachingBlocks.canonicalSolution:
Prompt: Your station is open. Pre-shift huddle just ended. You learned: a 60-top is on the books at 7 PM, a regular VIP is in at 6:30, and the produce delivery is short on a key item. With 30 minutes until first ticket, name the three positioning moves you make right now to absorb the load.

Expected response:
1. Pre-portion or pre-fire the items the 60-top will hit hardest, in batches sized to your hold capacity
2. Brief the expo and the lead on the short item so the menu call-out is consistent and substitutions are pre-decided
3. Stage tools and pans for the highest-volume item with extras within reach so you are not rotating mid-rush

Success criteria:
1. Cook anticipates load instead of reacting to it.
2. Cook synchronizes with expo and lead, not just within their own station.
3. Cook positions tools for volume, not for tidiness.
teachingBlocks.explanation:
Take a station that is technically open and turn it into a station that is actually ready to absorb tickets at a working pace. Open is not the same as ready.

The cook can identify the difference between an open station and a service-ready station, can read the board for the day's load, and can position tools and stock so the first ticket does not catch them flat-footed.

A station that is open passes a checklist. A station that is ready absorbs the next 30 minutes of tickets without panic. The difference is information and positioning. The cook reads the board, hears the pre-shift, and then makes three decisions: what to pre-fire or pre-portion, what to communicate up the chain, and where to put hands and tools so the highest-volume item builds itself. Cooks who skip the readiness pass are the ones who are technically clean during slow service and visibly underwater during a real rush.

Source data note: Generic readiness logic. Uncle Julio's specific pre-shift huddle format, board codes, and reservation-system data integration need authorized source.

teachingBlocks.title: Ticket Flow Basics
teachingBlocks.objective: Acknowledge fires audibly, identify the anchor item, and time shorter items backward so the plate lands together.
teachingBlocks.canonicalSolution:
Prompt: Expo fires a ticket: one item that takes 12 minutes, two items that take 6 minutes, one item that takes 90 seconds. You have to call your acknowledgment, identify the anchor, and decide when each item starts so the plate goes up together. Walk through it.

Expected response:
1. Acknowledge the fire out loud, audibly enough that expo confirms
2. Identify the 12-minute item as the anchor
3. Start the anchor first
4. Start the 6-minute items at the 6-minute mark of the anchor
5. Start the 90-second item with about 90 seconds left on the anchor
6. Plate together at the pass

Success criteria:
1. Acknowledgment is audible.
2. Anchor is correctly identified as the longest-cook item.
3. Other items are timed against the anchor, not started in parallel and held.
teachingBlocks.explanation:
Teach the cook to think about a ticket as a synchronized handoff with multiple owners, not as a private to-do list. The plate is judged at the pass; the cook is judged on whether their portion arrived on time and on standard.

The cook can identify the anchor item on a multi-item ticket, time secondary items against it, and acknowledge the expo audibly. The cook understands that finishing first is not winning if it means a held plate.

Every multi-item ticket has an anchor: the item that takes the longest to cook. Every other item on that ticket is timed backward from when the anchor will be ready. Cooks who do not think this way either start everything at once and hold most of it (which loses quality) or start late and finish late (which loses tables). Acknowledgment is not optional and not silent. The expo cannot route what they cannot hear, so the call goes up clearly and confirmed. Plating together at the pass is the standard; finishing your part first is not a win when the plate sits.

Source data note: Generic anchor logic. Uncle Julio's specific item timing standards (fajita timing, mesquite grill timing, tortilla press timing) require authorized source for accurate practice problems.

teachingBlocks.title: Downtime Decisions
teachingBlocks.objective: Prioritize restock, reset, and cleaning in the order that protects the next rush instead of the current appearance of the station.
teachingBlocks.canonicalSolution:
Prompt: The rush is over. You have about 12 minutes before the next push. The rail is half-empty, the station is messy but functional, and a deep cleaning task on your sidework list is overdue. List your priority order and explain why.

Expected response:
1. Restock the rail to par first
2. Reset and reorganize the station second
3. Tackle the deep-cleaning task last, only if the remaining window allows

Success criteria:
1. Restock is named first.
2. Cook articulates that an empty rail breaks faster than a messy station does.
3. Deep cleaning is treated as a downtime bonus, not a downtime priority.
teachingBlocks.explanation:
Train the cook to use the gap between rushes correctly. The next rush is decided in the previous gap, and the most common failure is doing the right things in the wrong order.

The cook can prioritize restock, reset, and clean correctly between rushes, and can articulate why restock comes first even when the station looks dirty.

Downtime is finite, and almost every kitchen has a default order that minimizes damage in the next rush. Restock first, because an empty rail kills tickets within seconds of a fire. Reset second, because a disorganized station accumulates errors throughout a service. Deep cleaning is the third priority — important, but not gating, and best done in pieces over many shifts rather than rushed before a push. Cooks who clean first because the station looks bad are responding to social pressure, not to operational reality. Managers who reward post-rush appearance over next-rush readiness train the wrong instinct.

Source data note: Generic priority logic. Uncle Julio's specific sidework lists, par sheets, and brand-specific deep-cleaning schedule need authorized source.

teachingBlocks.title: Cleaning and Reset
teachingBlocks.objective: Use micro-resets during service to remove hazards immediately without breaking ticket flow.
teachingBlocks.canonicalSolution:
Prompt: Mid-service. Tickets are still firing but slower. Your station has accumulated three sauté pans on the side, the cutting board has trim on it, and the sanitizer cloth on the counter is gray. In what order do you fix this without breaking ticket flow?

Expected response:
1. Refresh the sanitizer cloth first — a gray cloth is contaminating, not cleaning
2. Clear the cutting board of trim and wipe it down
3. Hand the spent sauté pans to the dish pit on your way back to the rail
4. Continue answering tickets between each micro-step so flow is not broken

Success criteria:
1. Cook recognizes a gray sanitizer cloth as a hazard, not a cosmetic issue.
2. Cook breaks reset into micro-steps that fit between tickets.
3. Cook does not stop ticket flow to do a full reset.
teachingBlocks.explanation:
Build the habit of resetting in the small gaps so the station never accumulates a deficit. Cleanliness is not a post-shift task; it is a continuous practice.

The cook can perform a mid-service reset without breaking ticket flow, can recognize when a sanitizer bucket has gone bad, and can hand off a clean station for the next shift.

Mid-service reset is a different skill than post-shift cleanup. The point is to keep the station functional without breaking ticket flow. A cook who tries to do a full reset between two tickets will miss the second ticket. A cook who never resets will be buried by the third. The right move is micro-steps: refresh the cloth between tickets, wipe the board between tickets, hand off pans on the path you were already walking. The question to ask before any mid-service action is: 'is this a hazard right now, or is it a cosmetic issue I can sweep into the next downtime window?' Hazards get fixed now; cosmetics wait.

Source data note: Generic. Uncle Julio's specific sanitizer concentration standards, brand-specific cleaning chemicals, and post-shift checklist need authorized source.

teachingBlocks.title: Assessment Gate: Service-Ready Cook
teachingBlocks.objective: Demonstrate full-service station control, chaos recovery, and downtime prioritization under live observation with no gating violations.
teachingBlocks.canonicalSolution:
Prompt: Live observation by a trainer or manager. The cook holds an assigned station through a service window that includes at least one ticket spike (chaos event), at least one downtime window, and at least one full ticket from fire to pass. The trainer signs off live, in person, on the AS7-final-pack-gate items.

Expected response:
1. Trainer sign-off on every item in AS7-final-pack-gate, with no gating violations on safe handling, color barriers, or audible communication.

Success criteria:
1. Cook acknowledges every fire audibly.
2. Cook anchors multi-item tickets correctly.
3. Cook recovers from at least one chaos event without manager intervention.
4. Cook prioritizes restock-reset-clean correctly during the downtime window.
5. No gating violations on safe handling or color barriers.
teachingBlocks.explanation:
Final gate. The cook either holds a station through a real service window with no gating violations, or they go back to the relevant module. There is no middle.

The cook is certified service-ready: they hold a station, recover from a chaos event, prioritize correctly during downtime, and can articulate one durable habit they have built during the pack.

The assessment gate is binary by design. A service-ready cook is one who can hold a station through a real service window without gating violations. Anything less means the cook is not yet service-ready, and the right answer is to send them back to the relevant module rather than pass them through with a borderline call. Pass-through certification creates cooks who fail later, often in front of guests. This gate is the contract: when the trainer signs off, the cook is on the line for real.

Source data note: Generic gate structure. Uncle Julio's specific certification authority (who is allowed to sign off), badge meaning in their HR system, and any tie-in to their training records platform need authorized source.

hints: This is a live observation. The trainer is reading you against the standard, not against the room.
If you fall behind, say so out loud. A cook who calls 'behind' early gets help. A cook who hides it gets buried.
The chaos drill is not a trick. The standard does not change because you are being observed.
